quiz.title: Chapter 15 Quiz: GenAI and Legal Research
quiz.intro: Ten questions on how these systems work, where they help, where they fail, and the one step the cycle adds.

items.q: Large language models produce citations that look real because they:
options: Predict, word by word, what is most likely to come next; a plausible citation has the same statistical shape as a real one
Are trained only on real opinions
items.why: The model cannot tell a true citation from a plausible false one (How Generative AI Works).

items.q: The single discipline the cycle adds for generative output is:
options: Use the tool only for drafting
Nothing enters your record unverified: every case, statute, quotation, and holding is checked against the primary source first
Ask the tool to confirm its answers
items.why: If you cannot find and read the source the system named, the answer does not exist (Running the Cycle Through an AI System).

items.q: Which question types does the chapter say generative AI handles best today?
options: Exploratory and focusing questions: orientation, vocabulary, settled standards
items.why: Application questions are where it fails most often and most convincingly (Generative AI Tools and the Research Cycle).

items.q: Why is a mega-prompt (“research my whole case”) a bad idea?
options: It produces a sprawling answer that is nearly impossible to verify, and errors compound across a long answer
items.why: One question, one checkable answer, one verification, then the next question (Generative AI Tools and the Research Cycle).

items.q: In Mata v. Avianca, where did the court locate the fault?
options: In using the tool at all
In the failure to verify and then in defending the fabrications once challenged
items.why: The lawyer asked the tool whether the cases were real; it said yes; he never looked (Example: What a fabricated citation costs).

items.q: In the demonstration’s third prompt, the tool returned Mahanoy, Papish, and Kennedy v. Bremerton. What went wrong?
options: The system lost sight of the specific question and returned results plausibly related to the general topic rather than responsive to the inquiry
items.why: The same false hit a human researcher caught in Chapter 3 (AI in Practice).

items.q: The AI research features built into Westlaw, Lexis+, and Bloomberg Law:
options: Have a lower risk profile because they work within verified databases, but the verification obligation does not change
items.why: Understanding that distinction is the first step in using AI responsibly (How Generative AI Works; Beyond the Basics).

items.q: When you log a verified AI answer, the chapter says to add to Source Consulted:
options: The system you used and the prompt you ran
items.why: And begin Findings with whether the answer was full, partial, or not really (Step 3).

items.q: Which is listed as an appropriate use without independent verification?
options: Summarizing a case you have already read and verified, or generating search terms and synonyms
Stating what the current law is
items.why: Citing any case, statute, or regulation from the tool requires verification (What Generative AI Can and Cannot Do).

items.q: If verifying an AI answer takes as long as finding it yourself would have, the chapter says:
options: That is data about the tool, and it belongs in your Notes field
items.why: Ask at every checkpoint whether the tool is still earning its place (The verification step; Exercise 15.3).
